title: Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg
content: At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities. The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five. A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit. Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday morning that Russia had targeted his country's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week. Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities - which it says are to limit the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort - for three days after the announcement, while accusing Russia of continuing. It then resumed strikes earlier this week, drawing the ire of Trump, who called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply diesel. Ukraine has struck St Petersburg before, though regions closer to Ukraine are threatened more often. The city's oil terminal was last hit in July . Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday. St Petersburg's governor said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the attacks on the city, while Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed. He also said mobile internet service disruption was possible. Social network VK confirmed a drone had targeted its regional data centre, but stressed its services were available "as usual" after users reported outages in the early hours of the morning. Ozon also confirmed its local logistics centre had been targeted by a drone, sparking a fire. It said staff were evacuated and no one was injured, and that it was not accepting shipments from sellers at the location "as it is currently serving other operational purposes". As well as numerous oil facilities across Russia, Ukraine has also mounted strikes aimed at disrupting the Russian economy more broadly. Earlier this month, it launched a series of attacks on Yandex, Russia's largest search engine, that led to service disruptions. Relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war, ahead of the midterm elections. Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort. Trump's decision to temporarily suspend a raft of sanctions against Russia has brought fresh criticism , including from some US Republicans. However, on Sunday, Zelensky said on Telegram he had had conversations with Trump's top negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. He said their teams are in constant communication and preparing the next diplomatic steps. Both Russia and Ukraine have been striking one another's energy infrastructure with increasing intensity ahead of the winter, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on in its fifth year. Russia says it hits targets used by Ukraine's military, though the UN noted on Friday that the first two weeks of October had been the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years. Russian strikes on energy facilities have left hundreds of thousands without power, raising concerns about civilians enduring another freezing winter. Zelensky said on Saturday that tens of thousands of people were still without power. Russia launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles in the past week, most of which were aimed at energy facilities, he said.

title: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day
content: Home sellers cut asking prices on more than 3,000 properties a day on average in Britain during September, according to figures from Rightmove shared exclusively with the BBC. The property website said the total was the highest of any month for 15 years and was driven, in part, by a glut of homes on the market and some sellers setting unrealistic expectations. The proportion of listed homes that eventually had a price cut peaked in 2023 and has remained relatively high since. Property portals say buyers are now having to be choosy, with many working to a tight budget as mortgage rates have risen to three-year highs. "Once a home has been on the market for a while and then has a price reduction, some buyers start asking questions, even when there is nothing wrong with the property," said Colleen Babcock of Rightmove. "In a market with so much choice, first impressions matter." Rightmove data said the average price reduction was nearly 7% - the equivalent of nearly £21,000 cut from a typically valued home. Its data showed that homes that had a price reduction typically took 119 days to find a buyer, compared with 39 days for those listed at one price. The proportion of listed homes that had a price reduction stood at 34% in last month, only slightly lower than the recent peak of 36% seen in September 2023. Rival property portal Zoopla said that buyers were in the driving seat, and were being more cautious and selective about the properties they viewed. With mortgage rates at a three-year high , Zoopla said buyers needed to keep monthly mortgage payments affordable. So, while the number of homes for sale was up 5% in September compared with a year earlier, the number of sales agreed had fallen by 9% over the same period, its figures showed. September also tends to be the month with the most cuts to asking prices as sellers often want to complete a sale by the end of the year. Zoopla's data showed that a quarter of newly-listed homes in September had previously been listed for sale in the last year. Six in 10 were returning at a lower asking price. The problem for sellers was that these homes were taking longer to sell. Properties that needed a price reduction were half as likely to find a buyer within the normal three-month timeframe, according to Richard Donnell, executive director of research at Zoopla. Sellers who have contacted the BBC's Your Voice have pointed to the difficulties created by lots of homes on the market, and extra problems for those selling leasehold properties in England. One, who was selling his late father's home in south Wales, said: "The market is dead. Lots for sale; no-one buying. No-one thinks it's going to get easier." Tarah Lourens, chief operating officer at Rightmove, said that "emotional" factors influenced sellers pricing a home - as they "put a value on the time and money they have invested in their home". But she said that buyers simply considered everything they could buy at their budget. Agents said that valuations now drew on huge amounts of data. Craig Webster, of Tiger Sales and Lettings in Blackpool, said that getting an initial price correct when new to the market was crucial. "That's when you have the greatest opportunity to capture the attention of active buyers," he said. Katie Griffin, from surveyors Sawdye and Harris in Devon, said that having to correct a price could ultimately lead to a seller accepting less than even a revised asking price. "The property may already have been online for several months and buyers can start asking why it has not sold," she said. But Andrew Boast, chief executive of SAM Conveyancing, said sellers might still not be losing out, if they had negotiated aggressively when buying the home and had seen it rise in value while they owned it. In Scotland, the Home Report system requires an independent valuation of a home before it is put on the market. Donnell, from Zoopla, said the system gave sellers a guide to pricing. As a result homes sold at a faster rate than anywhere else in Britain. His data showed that 74% of homes in Scotland listed during April, May and June sold within three months, compared with 30% in London. He said that higher prices, stamp duty and some people - including landlords - not needing to sell meant that listed homes were less likely to sell in southern England. The data provides insight into the market dynamics and buyer behavior, highlighting the impact of rising mortgage rates and the importance of first impressions. The article's findings are supported by data from two prominent property portals, Rightmove and Zoopla, making it a credible and informative piece for readers.

title: Microsoft pulls out of UK's largest AI data centre
content: A tech company has said it still plans to build the UK's largest AI data centre despite Microsoft pulling out of the project. Nscale announced last year it had pledged £2bn to build and open a pioneering facility in Loughton , Essex. However, the BBC understands that Microsoft, which said it would fund a supercomputer at the site, has terminated its involvement. A spokesperson for Nscale said it was exploring alternative power sources and its relationship with Microsoft remained strong for their other projects together overseas. Microsoft declined to comment. "We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK," Nscale said. "Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term." The data centre was due to receive its power supply at the end of the year. But as first reported by the Telegraph on Sunday , Nscale has been told this will not happen until the 2030s. "This unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," Nscale told the BBC. Nscale and Microsoft are still working together on projects in Norway, Portugal and the United States. The Loughton site is expected to create 250 permanent jobs when it eventually opens. Only last month, Microsoft announced that some of the $30bn (£22bn) it was investing in the UK would be used to fund the Loughton supercomputer. Do you have a story suggestion for Essex?
